subject: Tuesday the tariff on Canadian booze becomes a ban
bodyMarkdown:
At 12:01 a.m. Tuesday, a 50 per cent tariff on most Canadian alcohol turns into something else entirely: the goods are not allowed in at all. If you work at a distillery, a winery, a brewery, or anywhere along the truck route to Windsor, the price of your product stops being the question.

## What the ban actually covers

CNBC reported on September 9 that President Trump signed orders under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 barring imports of Canadian malt beer, wine, cider, whisky, vodka and other spirits, along with non-alcoholic beer, whey and molasses, certain dairy products, and motorcycles above 800 cc. Axios reported on September 8 that the measures carry no CUSMA exemption. The Globe and Mail reported that Canadian alcohol makes up 87.6 per cent of the banned list by dollar value. Bulk unpackaged wine slips through, though The Drinks Business reported this month that it still pays the 50 per cent duty. Goods that reached the border before Tuesday but have not yet been **entered for consumption**, the customs step that formally releases a shipment into the American market, stay on the duty rather than the ban, which is why trucks are still running this weekend.

## The numbers behind the noise

Canada's National Observer reported on September 10, citing Spirits Canada, that Canada exported $1.4 billion in alcoholic beverages to the United States in 2024-25, roughly 90 per cent of all Canadian alcohol exports, and that the spirits sector added about $5.8 billion to GDP in 2024 while supporting more than 48,800 full-time equivalent jobs. More than half the spirits Canadian distilleries make go south. That concentration is the whole problem. Moosehead chief executive Andrew Oland said he was "very disappointed," and noted that 15 per cent of the New Brunswick brewer's volume ships to the United States. Wine sits differently. Wine Growers B.C. president Jeff Guignard called the move "unprecedented and deeply frustrating," but only about 1 per cent of B.C. wine sales go to American buyers. Distillers have no cushion like that.

## Motorcycles and dairy are in it too

The Globe and Mail reported that BRP's Can-Am Spyder and Canyon, built in Valcourt, Quebec, will be shut out of the United States starting Tuesday, and that the company expects a $200-million net tariff hit this fiscal year and $225 million next. BRP says it is not cutting any of its 17,000 jobs and is not changing American prices. Ottawa is not sitting still either. The Globe reported this week that Canada put 50 per cent tariffs on large American motorcycles, which catches much of the Harley-Davidson lineup, while Washington added US$1.85 billion of Canadian goods to the Section 338 duty list. The Bank of Canada held at 2.25 per cent on September 2 and named tariffs as an upside risk to inflation, with Statistics Canada putting August inflation at 3.0 per cent.

## The takeaway

Watch Tuesday at 8:30 a.m., when Statistics Canada publishes July GDP, and read it as a baseline rather than a verdict, because the data predates everything that happens at midnight that morning. If you buy Canadian spirits in the States, the bottles on the shelf are the last of the inventory, since importers spent September racing shipments across. For anyone working in the sector, the Bank of Canada's October 28 decision matters less than whether Ottawa and Washington get back in a room, and nobody has said they will. I would plan on this still being true at Christmas.
